prize_parts.citation: for an oeuvre that renews lyric, essay and narrative through a living dialogue with antiquity, and that extends the book itself as a literary form.

statement.case_for: Carson's voice is among the most recognizable in contemporary writing in English. Her formal achievement is concrete and not merely a matter of novelty. Autobiography of Red turns the Geryon myth into a verse novel in which the line and the narrative arc work against each other. Nox makes elegy a matter of translation, archive and physical construction, and it is bound to a specific loss and to the limits of reading a dead brother and an ancient poem. The intellectual depth comes from long engagement with Greek and Latin literature. That engagement is part of the poetry's method and is not decoration. The work covers lyric, verse novel, essay, drama and translation, so the case rests on a whole body of work and not on one title. Her method has kept changing over decades, and this answers the concern about sustained quality. She also writes in English, so for a committee that depends on translation and expert reports for other languages, the linguistic judgment can be made directly. This is not a merit argument by itself. It does reduce one major source of uncertainty in the assessment. I keep Carson first after reading my colleagues, and I treat the objections to the citation scope as real but answerable.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the body of work is deliberately hybrid, and that the reputation may rest on a small number of landmark books more than on uniform quality across the corpus. Some of the work is occasional, fragmentary or dependent on physical format, and a citation would have to define the scope with care so that scholarship and translation are not credited as if they were the core original creation. If the committee judged that her hybrid forms do not amount to a sustained literary achievement in the sense of Nobel's will, Cărtărescu's larger and more continuous prose project, or Adonis's historically weighty renewal of a poetic language, would have the stronger case.

responses.point: Mattson places Cărtărescu first for a strongly individual visionary voice, with the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid forming an imaginative architecture. She asks, for Carson, whether the hybrid forms add up to sustained quality over the whole corpus, and she notes the risk that Cărtărescu's scale and recurring motifs read as repetition.
responses.response: I agree that Cărtărescu's architecture is the main literary argument for him, and I rank him third for that reason. I do not think her question about unevenness in Carson is decisive. Variety of method is part of the claim, and the books I regard as central, Autobiography of Red and Nox, stand on their language and construction. Mattson's own worry about repetition in Cărtărescu is the real point of difference. A work built on recurring obsessions needs to show development and not only accumulation, and I cannot settle that from translations of long, intricate Romanian prose. The question of scale versus development is one we should test further, and I would want to hear what the translated poetry and the earlier novels add.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first. He says a Carson citation would have to define its scope carefully, that genre labels are contested, and that it is uncertain whether the committee would treat the hybrid and book-object works as literature in the sense of Nobel's will. He also finds the durability of some later work harder to judge.
responses.response: I share the concern about scope, and I would make it a condition of any citation. I disagree that the book-object works put the claim at risk. In Nox the physical form is the vehicle for a text about translating Catullus and mourning a brother, and the claim stays a literary one. The citation should therefore rest on written language: the verse novel, the lyric and the essay. The physical form should be named only as an extension of what the book can do. I accept his point about the later work. My knowledge of it is partial, and I would not ask the committee to rely on my impression of recent books.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first. She says Carson's translations and classical adaptations could blur the boundary of what is credited as original creation, and that much of her reputation rests on a few landmark books.
responses.response: I agree that the boundary needs to be drawn, and I would draw it in the citation text. The translations and adaptations are part of how the original work arises, because Carson thinks through antiquity by translating it. That is evidence for the depth of the poetry and not a separate credit. The prize should name the original lyric, narrative and essayistic work. On her second point, the landmark-books concern holds for any candidate with a compact oeuvre, but Carson's output across several decades is wider than two titles. Whether the mid-career books and the shorter pieces reach the same level is the part I would want the committee to test against the corpus.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She puts Marilynne Robinson third, valuing a restrained, morally serious prose with a small but sustained fiction corpus. She also notes that Carson's translations and essays are hard to weigh against the original work.
responses.response: I agree with her on the difficulty of weighing translations and essays against original work. I would answer it as I did to Carlberg: the citation should rest on the original work. Robinson's case is real in the voice and in the coherence of the Gilead sequence. I place her lower than the other candidates because the fiction corpus is compact, and the breadth of significance across the whole body of work is a question here that I find less settled than for Carson or Cărtărescu. I would be glad to hear whether Palm considers the essays strong enough to bear weight in a citation, since that would change the question of breadth.

uncertainties: My knowledge of Carson's full corpus, especially later books, performance texts and translations, is partial and not independently verified.
The visual and typographic dimensions of Nox and similar works cannot be fully judged from description.
Whether the hybrid mode can be framed as a core literary achievement within Nobel's will is a judgment for the committee and is not settled by public information.
For Adonis, Cărtărescu, Can Xue and Tawada, linguistic achievement is judged through translation, so confidence in those assessments is limited. Expert reports could change them.
I cannot judge from the supplied evidence whether Cărtărescu's recurring imagery represents development or repetition across the whole body of work.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The documented connections (Horace Engdahl, Daniel Birnbaum, the Kris circle, and the Academy's co-opted secretaries) are not linked to any shortlisted writer. My own scholarly work on poetry, the fragment and exile is context and is not evidence that I favor any candidate.
